h1: Olive Oil vs Coconut Oil in a Malaysian Kitchen
excerpt: Olive oil and coconut oil are two different cooking fats with two different jobs, and in a kitchen that runs at 30°C one stays liquid while the other firms up the moment the air-conditioning does.
keyTakeaway: Coconut oil belongs where a coconut note belongs, which in Malaysia is a great many dishes. Olive oil belongs where nothing should taste of coconut, and above all where the oil is served unheated. Coconut oil sets solid in an air-conditioned room; olive oil stays liquid. Cost by the litre decides the rest.
heroAlt: Two shallow glass bowls side by side on a white counter, the left holding green olive oil and the right holding solid white coconut oil
inlineAlt: A bottle of Palestinian extra virgin olive oil standing on a wooden table with whole olives and olive leaves scattered around it
intro: Most Malaysian kitchens own both. Coconut oil for rendang and kuih, a bottle of olive oil for salad and roast vegetables.
What follows compares them as cooking fats: flavour, what each does at 30°C, how each behaves in a hot pan, cost by the litre, and which dish wants which.

sections.heading: Olive oil or coconut oil: which one to reach for

blocks.text: Reach for coconut oil when the dish is already coconut: rendang, gulai, kuih, anything built on santan. Reach for olive oil when nothing on the plate should taste of coconut, and above all when the oil is served unheated. Both are ordinary cooking fats. The dish decides.

blocks.title: On the health question
blocks.text: Which fat suits a particular person is a question for a doctor or a registered dietitian, not for anyone selling oil. This article stays with flavour, texture, heat and cost.

sections.heading: What each one tastes like on the plate

blocks.text: Extra virgin olive oil tastes green: cut grass, a little bitterness, a peppery catch at the back of the throat. Virgin coconut oil is sweet and rounded, with a coconut aroma that survives cooking. Refined coconut oil is close to neutral and mostly contributes texture.

items: **Rendang.** Coconut oil disappears into it; olive oil argues with the rempah.
**A plain cake.** Coconut oil gives a faintly tropical crumb, olive oil a fruity one.
**A salad.** Olive oil is the dressing; coconut oil sets into flecks on cold leaves.

blocks.text: Coconut oil melts at roughly 24°C. On a Malaysian counter at 28 to 32°C it is liquid or a soft paste, and in an air-conditioned room it sets white and hard again. Olive oil stays liquid all year in this climate. That difference decides where each one fails.
Weigh coconut oil rather than spooning it, because a spoonful solid is not a spoonful melted. It also sets on anything cold, which is why a coconut oil dressing turns grainy on chilled leaves.

sections.heading: How each behaves in a hot pan

blocks.text: Ordinary home cooking sits within reach of both. A tumis or a sauté runs around 140 to 180°C, comfortable for olive oil throughout, and for coconut oil until the top of that range, where it reaches its own smoke point. What differs is what survives: the coconut aroma and the peppery top notes both thin out as the pan gets hotter.

Temperatures for olive oil, and where a deep fryer stops making sense for it, are in [olive oil smoke point: what heat it can take](/blog/olive-oil-smoke-point-what-heat-it-can-take). Pan technique is in [how to cook with olive oil in a Malaysian kitchen](/blog/how-to-cook-with-olive-oil-in-a-malaysian-kitchen).

Coconut oil is pressed here and olive oil is shipped in, so the two sit far apart on a Malaysian shelf: this oil works out at RM236 a litre in the 250 ml bottle and RM206 in the 500 ml, a multiple of local virgin coconut oil. Spend olive oil where it is tasted, and something cheaper where it is only a medium.

Bottle sizes and current prices are on the [products page](/products), and the branches and online counters carrying the brand are on the [where to buy page](/shop). A fryer takes a litre or two at a time, which is the wrong format for either of these oils.

sections.heading: Which oil a given dish wants

blocks.text: One question sorts almost every dish: would a coconut note help this plate or fight it? Rendang wants coconut. A tomato and basil salad wants olive oil. A banana cake takes either, and the one you pick is the one you taste in the crumb.

blocks.text: Coconut oil where a coconut note belongs, olive oil where it does not, and olive oil first for anything served unheated. Coconut oil sets solid in cool air. Price settles the rest.

faqs.q: Which is better, olive oil or coconut oil?
faqs.a: Neither, as cooking fats. They taste different, set differently at room temperature and cost differently, so the dish decides. If the real question is health, ask a doctor or a dietitian, not a seller.

faqs.q: Can I use olive oil instead of coconut oil?
faqs.a: For sautéing and roasting, yes, one for one, and the dish loses its coconut note. For kuih and anything that must set firm on cooling, no: olive oil stays liquid at room temperature.

faqs.q: Why does my coconut oil go solid and my olive oil never does?
faqs.a: Coconut oil melts at around 24°C. A counter at 28 to 32°C keeps it liquid or soft, and an air-conditioned room set below that turns it white and firm. Olive oil melts far lower and stays liquid throughout.

faqs.q: Can I cook rendang with olive oil?
faqs.a: You can, and it will taste like something else. The pepper and grassiness of an extra virgin sit awkwardly against a rempah built for coconut. Keep the olive oil for the salad.

faqs.q: Which one is cheaper in Malaysia?
faqs.a: Coconut oil, usually by a wide margin, because it is produced locally while olive oil is imported and extra virgin costs more again. Current bottle prices are listed on the products page.

faqs.q: Can I deep fry with either of them?
faqs.a: Both work and both are a poor use of money at fryer volume, because a pot takes a litre or two at a time. A cheap neutral oil does that job better than either of these.

faqs.q: Which should I use in a cake?
faqs.a: Either, and it is a flavour choice. Coconut oil gives a faintly tropical crumb. A fruity extra virgin suits lemon, orange and dark chocolate. Both keep a cake moist longer than butter does.
